title: Safe Division Chain
story: Your calculator needs to chain operations safely. First divide 100 by 5 (safe!), then divide that result by 0 (danger!). Instead of crashing, you want each step to return either a valid number or an error, and the caller handles both. Chaining multiple safe operations is a real-world pattern.
why: Chaining Result-returning functions teaches error propagation � the backbone of reliable software.
analogy: Chaining safe operations is like a relay race. Each runner (operation) passes the baton (result value) to the next. If one runner drops the baton (error), the whole team is disqualified. The match expression is the handoff point.
try_it: Extend to a 3-step chain: divide A by B, then by C, then by D. Test it with 100/5/2/5 (should succeed), 100/0/2/5 (fail at step 1), and 100/5/0/5 (fail at step 2). Add a `safe_remainder` that also returns DivResult.
tips: Match on the intermediate result to peel out the Ok value before passing it to the next function
Return `DivResult.DivByZero` early in the error arm � don't try to continue the chain on failure
Name the error variant clearly: `DivByZero` tells callers exactly what went wrong
common_mistakes: Passing a `DivResult` directly to `safe_divide` � the function expects Int, not DivResult
Forgetting to handle the DivByZero case in the intermediate match � the match must be exhaustive
